newsitem.title: USA: U.S. decides to join Canada's anti-land-mine talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. decides to join Canada's anti-land-mine talks.

text.p: The United States on Monday threw its support behind a Canadian-backed process aimed at a global ban on land mines after a U.N. conference in Geneva failed to reach a breakthrough.

"The United States will participate in the Ottawa process negotiations on a treaty banning anti-personnel land mines," said a White House statement issued on the island of Martha's Vineyard, where President Bill Clinton was on vacation.
The Canadian initiative promises a treaty by the end of the year banning the use, export, production and stockpiling of anti-personnel land mines.

The problem is acute: U.S. officials estimate 9,600 people are killed by land mines worldwide every year and another 14,000 are wounded, double the number of injuries logged in 1980. Britain's Princess Diana recently drew attention to the problem.

Clinton had rejected the Canadian initiative in January after concluding it left little room for exceptions sought by U.S. military commanders. Instead, he made the U.N. Conference on Disarmament in Geneva the main focus of U.S. policy.
Critics of Geneva such as Sen. Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat, believe the U.N. process is too slow and rewards holdout nations.

A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said U.S. officials had been reviewing the results of the U.N. Conference on Disarmament since the last session ended in June and had concluded there was no significant progress there in the past six months.
The talks on drafting a final accord under the Ottawa process begin on Sept. 1 in Oslo.

"The United States is committed to pursuing the most promising opportunities for ending the use of anti-personnel land mines, which every year cause enormous suffering around the world," the White House statement said. The White House official insisted the United States was not abandoning the Geneva talks, saying they represented the best opportunity for a true, comprehensive global treaty, as opposed to the Canadian process, which does not include the biggest users and producers of land mines, like China and Russia.

"We've decided that we want to shift some of our effort over to the Ottawa process and work on both simultaneously. Our ultimate goal is a comprehensive global treaty. The only way to do that is through the U.N. Conference on Disarmament in Geneva. But those are very slow processes," the official said.

Laborious discussions in Geneva on a land mine ban have failed to make much progress, but Canada's invitation to meet in Ottawa and sign a treaty outlawing land mines later this year has drawn the backing of major U.S. allies.

Cambodia, Angola and Afghanistan are among more than 50 countries that have pledged support for Canada's "Ottawa process," which seeks to reach a treaty with as many signers as possible. China and Russia have said they will not sign.

The U.N.-sponsored conference in Geneva in May 1996 agreed to limit the use of some land mines but stopped short of a total ban because some countries argue they should remain a legitimate form of defense. Over 100 countries -- but not the United States -- have agreed to a total ban.

In Washington, State Department spokesman James Rubin said a U.S. delegation had gone to Geneva to meet with representatives of 17 countries to discuss how the United States could propose changes in the emerging Canadian agreement so Washington could support it in Oslo.

He said the United States wanted a "geographic exception" for its anti-personnel land mines on the Korean peninsula because "North Korean forces are on a high state of alert and there is always the risk of an attack from North Korea."
